readings.c3s1:
¶
'''whole''' (hōl), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''wholle''; with unorig. initial ''w''; prop., as in early mod. E., ''hole'', < ME. ''hol'', ''hool'', < AS. ''hāl'' = OS. ''hēl'' = OFries. ''hēl'' = D. ''heel'' = OHG. MHG. G. ''heil'', sound, whole, saved, = Icel. ''heill'' = Sw. ''hel'' = Dan. ''heel'' = Goth. ''hails'', hale, whole, = OBulg. ''cielŭ'', whole, complete; perhaps allied to Gr. καλός, excellent, good, hale, and Skt. ''kalya'', hale, healthy (> ''kalyāna'', prosperous, blessed). From ''whole'' (AS. ''hāl'') are also ult. E. ''wholesome'', ''wholesale'', ''wholly'', ''heal''<sup>1</sup>, ''health'', ''healthy'', and the second element of ''wassail''; from the Scand. form (Icel. ''heill'') are ult. E. ''hale''<sup>2</sup>, ''hail''<sup>2</sup>, etc. The change of initial ''ho-'' to ''who-'' was a dial. peculiarity, there being an actual change of pronunciation (hō to hwō), due to the labializing effect of the long ō; the change was reflected in the spelling, which in some words, as ''whole'', ''whoop'', ''whore'', ''whot'', came into literary use, while the orig. pronunciation with simple ''h'' remained or prevailed. In dial. use the ''who-'' (''hwo-'') thus developed was afterward reduced in some districts to ''wo-'', as ''wot'' for ''whot'' (orig. ''whote'') for ''hot'' (orig. ''hote''). ''Whole'' is one of the words which the American Philological Association and the English Philological Society include in their list of spellings to be amended, recommending the restoration of the old form ''hole'', in keeping with the derived or related ''holy'', ''heal''<sup>1</sup>, ''hale''<sup>2</sup>, etc. (Trans. Amer. Philol. Ass., 1886, p. 127).] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Hale; healthy; sound; strong; well.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|who|6915|whole}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|<poem>He nadde bote a dogter ''ho'' mygte ys eir be.</poem>
{{right|''Rob. of Gloucester'', p. 89.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Witnesse on Job ''whom'' that we diden wo.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Friar’s Tale, l. 193.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A verse may find him ''who'' a sermon flies.</poem>
{{right|''G. Herbert'', The Church Porch.}}}}
{{smaller block|The general purposes of men in the conduct of their lives . . . end in gaining either the affection or the esteem of those with ''whom'' they converse.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 206.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Grant me still a friend in my retreat,
''Whom'' I may whisper — solitude is sweet.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Retirement, l. 742.}}}}

The antecedent is sometimes omitted, being implied in the pronoun, which is in this case usually called a ''compound relative.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Adraweth ȝoure suerdes & loke ''wo'' may do best.</poem>
{{right|''Rob. of Gloucester'', l. 127 (Morris and Skeat, II. 6).}}}}
{{smaller block|Ac hi casten heore lot ''hwes'' he [Christ’s garment] scolde beo. {{right|''Old Eng. Misc.'' (ed. Morris), p. 50.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Now tell me ''who'' made the world.</poem>
{{right|''Marlowe'', Faustus, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The dead man’s knell
Is there scarce ask’d for ''who.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3. 171.}}}}
{{smaller block|There be ''who'' can relate his domestic life to the exactness of a diary. {{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xxvii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Her we ask’d of that and this,
And ''who'' were tutors.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, i.}}}}

(2) A clause dependent in form, but adding a distinct idea. Here the relative force is almost entirely lost, ''who'' becoming equivalent to ''and'' with a demonstrative pronoun.
{{smaller block|<poem>He trod the water,</poem>}}
<poem>''Whose'' enmity he flung aside.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 1. 116.}}}}

{{smaller block|The yong man . . . at last married her, to ''whose'' wedding, amongst other guests, came Apollonius, who . . . found her out to be a Serpent, a Lamia.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 438.}}}}

(''b'') With reference to gender, ''who'' originally noted a masculine or feminine antecedent, whether human, animate, or other, the neuter being ''what;'' and ''whose'', the possessive (genitive) of ''who'', was also that of ''what'', and is still correctly used of a neuter antecedent (see ''what''<sup>1</sup>). Moreover, before the appearance of the possessive ''its'', whose place was filled by the neuter ''his'' (see ''he''<sup>1</sup>, I., C. (''b'')), not only were neuter objects designated in the two other cases by ''he'' and ''him'', but ''who'' and ''whom'' were sometimes substituted for ''that'' as the nominative and objective of the neuter relative (see the quotation from Puttenham). In modern use, however, ''who'' and ''whom'' are applied regularly to persons, frequently to animals, and sometimes even to inanimate things when represented with some of the attributes of humanity, as in personification or vivid description.

<poem>Men seyn over the walle stonde
Grete engynes, ''who'' were nygh honde.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 4194.}}}}

{{smaller block|The nature and condition of man . . . is called humanitie; whiche is a generall name to those vertues in ''whome'' semeth to be a mutuall concorde and loue in the nature of man. {{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, ii. 8.}}}}

{{smaller block|Such is the figure Ouall, ''whom'' for his antiquitie, dignitie and vse, I place among the rest of the figures to embellish our proportions. {{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 84.}}}}

<poem>Death arrests the organ of my voice,
''Who'', entering at the breach thy sword hath made,
Sacks every vein and artier of my heart.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Marlowe'', Tamburlaine, I., ii. 7.}}}}

<poem>A green and gilded snake . . .
''Who'' with her head nimble in threats approach’d
The opening of his mouth.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iv. 3. 110.}}}}

{{smaller block|Two things very worthy the obseruation I saw in two of the walkes, euen two beech trees, ''who'' were very admirable to behold, not so much for the height, . . . but for their greatnesse.{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 37.}}}}

{{smaller block|Animals, ''who'', by the proper application of rewards and punishments, may be taught any course of action.{{right|''Hume'', Human Understanding, ix.}}}}

{{smaller block|If strange dogs come by, . . . she [a doe] returns to the cows, ''who'', with fierce lowings and menacing horns, drive the assailants quite out of the pasture.{{right|''Gilbert White'', Nat. Hist. Selborne, xxiv.}}}}

{{smaller block|A mirror for the yellow-billed ducks, ''who'' are seizing the opportunity of getting a drink.{{right|''George Eliot'', Adam Bede, vi.}}}}

<poem>And you, ye stars,
''Who'' slowly begin to marshal,
As of old, in the fields of heaven,
Your distant, melancholy lines!</poem>{{right|''M. Arnold'', Empedocles on Etna, ii.}}

(c) With reference to the nature of its antecedent, ''who'' may note—(1) a particular or determinate person or thing (see (''a'')); or (2) an indefinite antecedent, in which case ''who'' has the force of ''whoso'', ''whosoever'', or ''whoever'', and is called an ''indefinite relative''. Its antecedent may be expressed, or it may be a compound relative.

<poem>''Hwam'' ich biteche that bred that ich on wyne wete,
He me schal bitraye.</poem>{{right|''Old Eng. Misc.'' (ed. Morris), p. 40.}}

<poem>''Quos'' deth so he deȝyre he dreped als faste.</poem>{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 1648.}}

<poem>Of croice in the alde testament
Was mani bisening [tokens], ''qwa'' to cowde tent.</poem>{{right|''Holy Rood'' (ed. Morris), p. 118.}}

<poem>“''Whom'' the gods love die young,” was said of yore.</poem>{{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, iv. 12.}}

'''As who saith.''' Same as ''as who should say.''

<poem>For he was synguler hym-self, and seyde faciamus,
''As who seith'' more mote here-to than my worde one.</poem>{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), ix. 36.}}

<poem>My maister Bukton, whan of Criste our Kinge
Was axed what is trouthe or sothfastnesse,
He nat a word answerde to that axinge,
''As who saith,'' “no man is al trew,” I gesse.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Envoy of Chaucer to Bukton, l. 4.}}}}

'''As who should say''', as one who says or who might say; as if one should say.

{{smaller block|He doth nothing but frown, ''as who should say,'' “If you will not have me, choose.”
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 2. 51.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The slave . . . holds
John Baptist’s head a-dangle by the hair,
With one hand (“look you, now,” ''as who should say'').</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Fra Lippo Lippi.}}}}

'''The who''', that one who; who: so also ''the whose, the whom.'' [Archaic.]

{{smaller block|''The whos'' power as now is falle.
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., v.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Your mistress, from ''the whom'', I see,
There ’s no disjunction to be made.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 4. 539.}}}}

'''Who all''', all the persons who; the whole number (who). [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|I don’t know ''who all'', for I aint much of a bookster and don’t recollect.
{{right|''Haliburton'', Sam Slick in England, xlviii.}}}}

'''Who but he''', who else? he only; nobody else.

{{smaller block|Every one repaireth to Wriothesley, honoureth Wriothesley (as the Assyrians did to Haman), and all things as done by his advice: and ''who but he?''
{{right|''Ponet'', quoted in R. W. Dixon’s Hist. Church of Eng.,}}
{{right|[xvi., note.}}}}
{{smaller block|She made him Marquis of Ancre, one of the Twelve Mareschals of France, Governor of Normandy; and confered divers other Honours and Offices of Trust upon him: and ''who but he?''
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. i. 19.}}}}

'''Who that†''', who or whoever: as a relative, either definite or indefinite.

<poem>For ''who that'' entreth ther,
He his sauff euere-more.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''William of Shoreham'', De Baptismo, l. 6 (Morris and Skeat, [II. 63).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And dame Musyke commaunded curteysly
La Bell Pucell wyth me than to daunce,
''Whome that'' I toke wyth all my plesaunce.</poem>
{{right|''Hawes'', Pastime of Pleasure (Percy Soc.), p. 70.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Who, which,'' and ''that'' agree in being relatives, and are more or less interchangeable as such; but ''who'' is used chiefly of persons (though also often of the higher animals), ''which'' almost only of animals and things (in old English also of persons), and ''that'' indifferently of either, except after a preposition, where only ''who'' or ''which'' can stand. Some recent authorities teach that only ''that'' should be used when the relative clause is limiting or defining: as, the man ''that'' runs fastest wins the race; but ''who'' or ''which'' when it is descriptive or coördinating: as, this man, ''who'' ran fastest, won the race; but, though present usage is perhaps tending in the direction of such a distinction, it neither has been nor is a rule of English speech, nor is it likely to become one, especially on account of the impossibility of setting ''that'' after a preposition; for to turn all relative clauses into the form “the house ''that'' Jack lived ''in''” (instead of “the house ''in which'' Jack lived”) would be intolerable. In good punctuation the defining relative is distinguished (as in the examples above), by never taking a comma before it, whether it be ''who'' or ''which'' or ''that.'' Wherever ''that'' could be properly used, but only there, the relative may be, and very often is, omitted altogether: thus, the house Jack built or lived in; the man (or the purpose) he built it for. The adjective clause introduced by a relative may qualify a noun in any way in which an adjective or adjective phrase, either attributive or appositional, can qualify it, and has sometimes a pregnant implication of one or another kind: as, why punish this man, ''who'' is innocent? i. e. seeing, or although, he is innocent (= this innocent man). But a relative is also not rarely made use of to add a coördinate statement, being equivalent to ''and'' with a following pronoun: as, I studied geometry, ''which'' I found difficult (''and'' [''I''] found ''it'' difficult); I met a friend, ''who'' kindly showed me the way (''and he'' kindly, etc.). This way of employing the relative is by some regarded as a Latinism, and condemned; it is restricted to ''who'' and ''which''.}}

'''whoa''' (hwō), ''interj.''   [A var. of ''ho''<sup>1</sup>.]   Stop! stand still!
{{smaller block|Come, Ile go teach ye hayte and ree, gee and ''whoe'', and which is to which hand.
{{right|''Heywood'', Fortune by Land and Sea (Works, ed. 1874, VI. 384).}}}}

'''whobub†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''hubbub''. Also ''whoobub.''
{{smaller block|<poem>[Cry within of Arm, Arm!
What a vengeance ails this ''whobub?'' pox refuse ’em.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Women Pleased, iv. 1.}}}}

'''whode†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''hood.''
{{smaller block|I maruell that he sent not therwith a foxes tayle for a scepture, and a ''whode'' with two eares.
{{right|''Bp. Bale'', English Votaries, fol. 104.}}}}

'''whoever''' (hö-ev′ėr), ''indef. pron.''   [< ''who'' + ''ever.'']   Any person whatever; no matter who; any one without exception.
{{smaller block|Forsoth by a solemne day he was wont to leeue to hem oon bounden, ''whom euere'' thei axiden. ''Wyclif'', Mark xv. 6.
<poem>''Whoever'' bound him, I will loose his bonds.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., v. 1. 339.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Whoever'' in those glasses looks may find
The spots return’d, or graces, of his mind,
And by the help of so divine an art,
At leisure view and dress his nobler part.</poem>
{{right|''Waller'', Upon B. Jonson.}}}}
{{smaller block|I will not march one foot against the foe till you all swear to me that ''whomever'' I take or kill his arms I shall quietly possess. {{right|''Swift'', Battle of Books.}}}}

'''whole''' (hōl), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''wholle''; with unorig. initial ''w''; prop., as in early mod. E., ''hole'', < ME. ''hol'', ''hool'', < AS. ''hāl'' = OS. ''hēl'' = OFries. ''hēl'' = D. ''heel'' = OHG. MHG. G. ''heil'', sound, whole, saved, = Icel. ''heill'' = Sw. ''hel'' = Dan. ''heel'' = Goth. ''hails'', hale, whole, = OBulg. ''cielŭ'', whole, complete; perhaps allied to Gr. καλός, excellent, good, hale, and Skt. ''kalya'', hale, healthy (> ''kalyāna'', prosperous, blessed). From ''whole'' (AS. ''hāl'') are also ult. E. ''wholesome'', ''wholesale'', ''wholly'', ''heal''<sup>1</sup>, ''health'', ''healthy'', and the second element of ''wassail''; from the Scand. form (Icel. ''heill'') are ult. E. ''hale''<sup>2</sup>, ''hail''<sup>2</sup>, etc. The change of initial ''ho-'' to ''who-'' was a dial. peculiarity, there being an actual change of pronunciation (hō to hwō), due to the labializing effect of the long ō; the change was reflected in the spelling, which in some words, as ''whole'', ''whoop'', ''whore'', ''whot'', came into literary use, while the orig. pronunciation with simple ''h'' remained or prevailed. In dial. use the ''who-'' (''hwo-'') thus developed was afterward reduced in some districts to ''wo-'', as ''wot'' for ''whot'' (orig. ''whote'') for ''hot'' (orig. ''hote''). ''Whole'' is one of the words which the American Philological Association and the English Philological Society include in their list of spellings to be amended, recommending the restoration of the old form ''hole'', in keeping with the derived or related ''holy'', ''heal''<sup>1</sup>, ''hale''<sup>2</sup>, etc. (Trans. Amer. Philol. Ass., 1886, p. 127).]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Hale; healthy; sound; strong; well. {{smaller block|<poem>When his men saw hym ''hol'' and sounde,
For sothe they were ful fayne.</poem>
{{right|''Robin Hood and the Monk'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 15).}}}}
{{smaller block|They that be ''whole'' need not a physician, but they that are sick.{{right|Mat. ix. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A soul . . .
So healthy, sound, and clear and ''whole.''</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Miller’s Daughter.}}}}
'''2.''' Restored to a sound state; healed; made well.
{{smaller block|What Man that first bathed him, aftre the mevynge of the Watre, was made ''hool'' of what maner Sykenes that he hadde.{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 88.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thy faith hath made thee ''whole;'' go in peace, and be ''whole'' of thy plague.{{right|Mark v. 34.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He call’d his wound a little hurt,
Whereof he should be quickly ''whole.''</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}
'''3.''' Unimpaired; uninjured; unbroken; intact: as, the dish is still ''whole;'' to get off with a ''whole'' skin.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fier brennen on the grene leaf,
And thog grene end ''hol'' bi-leaf.</poem>
{{right|''Genesis and Exodus'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2776.}}}}
{{smaller block|My life is yet ''whole'' in me.{{right|2 Sam. i. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet all goes well, yet all our joints are ''whole.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iv. 1. 83.}}}}
'''4.''' Entire; complete; without omission, reduction, diminution, etc.: as, a ''whole'' apple; the ''whole'' duty of man; to serve the Lord with one’s ''whole'' heart; three ''whole'' days; the ''whole'' body.
{{smaller block|For all the ''hole'' temple is dedycate and halowed in the honour and name of the holy Sepulcre.{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|Ther is a parte of the hede of Seynt George, hys left Arme with the ''holl'' hande. {{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whole'' we call that, and perfect, which hath a beginning, a midst, and an end. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Discoveries.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Assassination, her ''whole'' mind
Blood-thirsting, on her arm reclin’d.</poem>
{{right|''Churchill'', The Duellist, iii. 67.}}}}
{{smaller block|Of the disgraceful dealings which were . . . kept up with the French Court, Danby deserved little or none of the blame, though he suffered the ''whole'' punishment.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Sir William Temple.}}}}
'''5.''' All; every part, unit, or member required to make up the aggregate: as, the ''whole'' city turned out to receive him.
{{smaller block|Yeis arn ye ordynnaunces of our Gylde, ordeynd be alle the ''hol'' fraternite. {{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 103.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''whole'' race of mankind. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., iv. 1. 40.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''whole'' Anglican priesthood, the ''whole'' Cavalier gentry, were against him. {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vii.}}}}
'''6†.''' Without reserve; sincerely or entirely devoted.
{{smaller block|<poem>Have, and ay shal, how sore that me smerte,
Ben to yow trew and ''hool'' with al myn herte.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 1001.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Sheriff is noght so ''hole'' as he was, for now he wille shewe but a part of his frendeshippe.
{{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 208.}}}}
'''7†.''' Unified; in harmony or accord; one.
{{smaller block|I think of you as of God’s dear children, whose hearts are ''whole'' with the Lord.
{{right|''J. Bradford'', Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 40.}}}}
'''8.''' In ''mining'', that part of a coal-seam in process of being worked in which the headings<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
